metadata.title: Why Web Search Never Runs Your Code but Your Own Tool Always Does — with Identical Syntax
metadata.purpose: Answer one real question in the Teardown register: why does web search finish inside one request while your own tool call always needs two, when both are declared the same way? Lands the carry-out that round-trip count is set by who can execute, not by how the tool is declared.
metadata.anchor_pair: B02 -> B04 (.webSearch/serverTools vs lookupFavorites/tools declaration case, paid off with the osmosis/checkNotes example plus both directions)

beats.narration_text: Someone declares two tools the same way, in the same file, and gets two completely different round-trip behaviors back from Claude. That's not a bug in the SDK — it's the boundary of who can execute.

beats.narration_text: Declaring a tool feels uniform. You list it, Claude sees it, Claude can call it — one file, one syntax, one API surface. So the natural mental model is one execution path: the model emits a call, your code runs it, you send the answer back. That path is real for the tools you wrote. It was never real for web search.

shot.new_visual_element: A single 'declare a tool' card branching into two identical-looking call shapes; one keeps its emit-run-send loop, the other's loop breaks open

production_viz.label: Same declaration, different behavior
production_viz.mechanic: One 'DECLARE A TOOL' card at top branches into two identical call shapes below it, each a closed loop labelled EMIT → RUN → SEND BACK. The right-hand loop cracks open at RUN, in terracotta, with a small 'not true for web search' caption.

beats.narration_text: Here's the concrete case. In one Swift file, `.webSearch(maxUses: 5)` goes into `serverTools`; `lookupFavorites()` goes into `tools`. Same declaration syntax. But the two arrays route to different runtimes. `serverTools` executes inside Anthropic's turn — the answer is already on the response you receive. `tools` emits a tool-use block your own app has to see, run, and reply to. The array name is doing the work the syntax hides.

shot.new_visual_element: THE ANCHOR -- two declaration cards side by side, serverTools/.webSearch and tools/lookupFavorites(), one path closes on itself, the other exits to a labelled 'your app' box

production_viz.label: THE ANCHOR -- serverTools vs. tools
production_viz.mechanic: THE ANCHOR. Left mono card: `serverTools: [.webSearch(maxUses: 5)]` labelled SERVER-SIDE. Right mono card: `tools: [lookupFavorites()]` labelled CLIENT-SIDE. From the left card a short arrow loops back to a CLAUDE label. From the right card an arrow exits to a box labelled YOUR APP, captioned 'only your app can run this'. THIS COMPOSITION RETURNS AT B04.

beats.narration_text: Round-trip count comes down to a single question: who can execute this. Web search needs a live crawler index and a sandbox — infrastructure Anthropic already runs — so the model finishes the call inside the same turn. `lookupFavorites()` is arbitrary Swift on your device; nobody upstream can run it. The model emits the request, halts, and waits for a second HTTP request to carry the answer back. Anthropic optimized for in-turn latency on the tools they hold; yours can't finish in-turn, ever.

shot.new_visual_element: Two lanes: ANTHROPIC'S SERVERS closing its own loop; YOUR DEVICE, its arrow exiting the frame and re-entering as a second request

production_viz.label: Who can execute
production_viz.mechanic: Left lane: ANTHROPIC'S SERVERS, with small index and sandbox icons, a single arrow looping back on itself labelled 'closes in-turn'. Right lane: YOUR DEVICE, an arrow that exits the frame's edge (terracotta) and re-enters lower down labelled 'second request'.

beats.narration_text: Say to Claude, "search osmosis, then check my notes." The search resolves inside that one request — no callback into your code. `checkNotes()` can't: the model emits the call, your code runs it, a separate HTTP request carries the answer back. Two knobs don't change this. Function size — even a one-line `checkNotes()` still forces the round trip; the boundary is trust and execution, not lines. Call frequency — web search can fire once or ten times, every hit resolves in-turn, because Anthropic still holds the sandbox. Who executes decides the round trip. Not how the tool is declared.

shot.new_visual_element: THE ANCHOR RETURNS -- the osmosis search closes its own loop; checkNotes() exits and re-enters; both-directions captions

production_viz.label: THE ANCHOR RETURNS -- one boundary, tested both ways
production_viz.mechanic: THE B02 COMPOSITION RETURNS: the SERVER-SIDE card's loop now carries the label 'search osmosis' and closes cleanly on CLAUDE. The CLIENT-SIDE card's arrow now carries 'checkNotes()', exits to YOUR APP, and a second arrow returns captioned 'answer back'. Beneath, two small captions: 'trivial function — still round-trips' under the client side, 'fires twice — still in-turn' under the server side.

beats.narration_text: It isn't the syntax that decides the round trip — it's who holds execution. Anthropic runs its own tools inside the turn; only your app can run yours, so the model stops and waits for a second request to bring the answer back.

beats.narration_text: Your turn. Paste this into Claude, ChatGPT, or Gemini. I'm designing an app that mixes server-side tools like web search with my own client-side tools. Walk me through what happens at the network level for each — how many round-trips, who executes the tool, and where the result enters the conversation — so I can size latency budgets. Then go deeper: ask the same model which of your client-side tools you'd redesign as a server-side capability, and what you'd give up moving them out of your own process. Liam, in for Bear.
